prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual contributions to understanding how technological change, task content and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged, and so are the reasons for it. B014 gives a clear conceptual frame (skill-biased change, the education-technology race, task-based labour demand). Its empirical designs are transparent and have been exposed to re-analysis for a long time. The skill-premium findings have been reproduced across countries and periods. The China-shock designs have been replicated, re-examined and criticised for about a decade. The qualitative conclusion, that adjustment costs are concentrated and persistent in exposed local labour markets, has survived, even though the magnitudes are still debated. I give most weight to how well a result has been confronted with data and has survived. By that criterion I rate B014 above candidates whose key mechanism is identified more indirectly. The topic also bears on current debates about automation and AI. The three names map onto separable contributions: Autor spans both strands, Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz anchors the long-run skill-premium literature. The round-1 exchange did not change my view of B014's merit. It did sharpen my view of which alternative I would support, and I say so openly below. This is not a search for consensus.
statement.case_against: B014 may be two achievements, task-based technology change and trade shocks, and a three-name cap cannot cover both cleanly. Dorn is a core co-author on the trade-shock papers and is left out. Part of the task-framework theory belongs to Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not credited. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still contested. Colleagues also note thematic proximity to the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I think this is a framing issue and not a duplication, but it makes the marginal credit harder to isolate. Finally, only one file prefers B014 as the single part, and I do not regard that count as evidence of merit either way. The chair's summary, though, shows that B014 is unlikely to reach six votes as things stand. A committee that valued clean two-name attribution and a settled verdict could reasonably put B011 or B005 ahead of it.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B011 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises covers related but distinct ground, and that the collateral-price feedback is a clean two-author mechanism. In his own B014 proposal he would credit Autor, Hanson and Dorn and treats Katz as part of the older skill-biased tradition.
responses.response: Your account of the 2022 overlap has moved me. Bank runs and bank-specific information problems are a different object from collateral-driven amplification in the real economy, so I now treat that overlap as a wording matter and not a strong reason to demote B011. My remaining reservation is the one you list yourself: the size of the collateral channel is identified indirectly. I count that as a real limit on how confidently one can say what the result has established empirically, but it does not make the mechanism less foundational. If B014 cannot carry, B011 is the single part I would support. On Dorn versus Katz, I still hold Katz because the skill-premium work is what makes B014 a labour-demand discovery. A purely trade-shock citation would be the case for Dorn, and I would want the committee to choose between the two framings explicitly.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 with Helpman and Melitz. He wants the citation anchored on selection and reallocation across firms and not on the empirical discovery of exporter heterogeneity. He also argues that Bernard and Jensen's exporter-premium facts and the Eaton-Kortum strand do not make the two-person proposal indefensible.
responses.response: This answers part of my attribution worry. A citation that names the theoretical integration of firm heterogeneity into trade, and does not claim the exporter-premium facts, is a defensible way to handle the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum gap. I now regard that gap as manageable through wording. I still place B005 behind B011 in my fallback order. Its attribution is less clean than a single 1997 paper, and the Helpman credit has to be separated from Krugman's 2008 recognition and from the separate B020 entry. In its favour, B005 is the candidate whose core selection mechanism has been tested most directly on firm-level data, and that matters a great deal to me. The two are close for me, and I would not treat a vote for B005 as unreasonable.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B011 and lists B014 as her first alternative. She calls it the strongest labour candidate. She qualifies this by saying that the China-shock effects are still debated, that the task framework sits close to the 2023 and 2024 prizes, and that she would still choose Katz over Dorn for a three-person group.
responses.response: I accept your qualifications. They are the weaknesses I list myself, and I think they explain why B014 has support from you as an alternative but not as a first choice. I would answer only on the overlap point. I read the 2023 citation as being about women's labour-market history and the 2024 citation as being about institutions and prosperity, so the link to task-based labour demand is thematic. Even so, I concede that a committee seeing the area as recently honoured would find it harder to justify B014. I also agree with you on Katz. Your own case for B011, with its stress on a mechanism that others have reused, is persuasive, and I do not treat the number of B011 first places as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B011 and holds that Kiyotaki and Moore are the singular origin of the collateral-price mechanism. He places B005 second and says the two are close. For B014 he would credit only Autor and Hanson, noting that the task theory owes much to Acemoglu and Restrepo.
responses.response: I take your point that attribution is the strongest feature of B011, and I now regard it as my preferred fallback. On B014 I am not persuaded to go to two names, because dropping Katz would remove the oldest and most replicated findings in the file. I do agree that the task-theory credit is partly outside our names. That is why I word the citation around empirical and conceptual contributions and not around a task model. Your observation that the case for B011 rests on reuse as a modelling building block, and not on a measured magnitude, is also the point on which I would insist on careful citation wording: the citation should honour the mechanism and not claim a quantified effect.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the task/technology and trade-shock strands as one achievement or two, and whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name.
How much of the task-framework credit sits with Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not among the credited names.
The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the long-run reading may change.

Whether, if B014 does not reach six votes, the collateral channel's indirect identification (B011) or the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Krugman 2008 attribution questions (B005) are the less serious problem. I currently judge B011's attribution to be cleaner, and B005's firm-level testing to be more direct.
My assessments rely on general knowledge and the supplied committee text. I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and networks (Johannesson, Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Brodeur and the Institute for Replication, and the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics group) lie in metascience and experimental economics. The profile shows no tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Dorn, Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz or Redding. My metascience and replication interests could incline me to favour work with a strong record of re-analysis, and I note that as a possible bias. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
